questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis with indurated edges and a clean base, followed by painless inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this condition?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: The presentation is classic primary syphilis (chancre). Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose is the drug of choice for primary and secondary syphilis as per WHO and CDC guidelines.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops tense bullae on normal-appearing skin, mostly on flexural areas. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. Which antigen is primarily targeted?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid is characterised by tense bullae on flexural areas. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at DEJ. The target antigens are BP230 (intracellular hemidesmosomal protein) and BP180 (transmembrane collagen XVII), components of the hemidesmosome.

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer from Bihar presents with well-defined hypopigmented patches with complete sensory loss and palpable thickened ulnar nerve. Slit-skin smear is negative. What is the most appropriate classification and treatment regimen?
opts: Paucibacillary leprosy — Rifampicin 600 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months
Multibacillary leprosy — Rifampicin 600 mg + Clofazimine 300 mg monthly + Dapsone 100 mg + Clofazimine 50 mg daily for 12 months
Paucibacillary leprosy — Rifampicin 600 mg monthly alone for 6 months
Indeterminate leprosy — Dapsone 100 mg daily for 12 months
questions.exp: Fewer than 5 lesions with negative SSS = paucibacillary (PB) leprosy. WHO MDT for PB leprosy: Rifampicin 600 mg supervised monthly + Dapsone 100 mg daily for 6 months.

questions.q: A 22-year-old female presents with malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and arthralgia. ANA is 1:640 (homogeneous). Anti-dsDNA is positive. Which skin finding is MOST specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) plaques — scarring, follicular plugging, hypopigmentation/hyperpigmentation — are the most specific cutaneous manifestation of lupus erythematosus, though they can occur without systemic disease. The malar rash is characteristic but less specific.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a slow-growing, pearly-white nodule with central ulceration and rolled, telangiectatic borders on the nose. Histology shows palisading peripheral nuclei with retraction artefact. What is the most appropriate primary treatment?
questions.exp: This is basal cell carcinoma (BCC) of the nose — a high-risk site. Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (99%) with maximal tissue sparing, making it the preferred treatment for BCC at cosmetically and functionally critical sites.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple painless, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication scattered over the face, trunk, and genitalia. CD4 count is 80 cells/µL. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by MCV, a poxvirus. In severely immunocompromised HIV patients (CD4 <200), lesions are atypically numerous, large, and facial. Effective antiretroviral therapy is the cornerstone of management.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child presents with boggy, fluctuant scalp swelling with satellite pustules, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and patchy alopecia. KOH examination of broken hair stubs shows arthroconidia arranged in a mosaic pattern (ectothrix). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Kerion celsi is an inflammatory tinea capitis presenting as a boggy mass with pustules. Microsporum canis causes large-spore ectothrix infection. The mosaic ectothrix pattern on KOH and the zoophilic source (cats/dogs) point to M. canis.

questions.q: A patient with longstanding psoriasis is started on methotrexate. Which investigation is the GOLD STANDARD for monitoring methotrexate hepatotoxicity in psoriasis patients?
opts: Serum liver function tests every 3 months
Liver biopsy after cumulative dose of 1–1.5 g
questions.exp: Liver biopsy after a cumulative methotrexate dose of 1–1.5 g (or after every additional 1–1.5 g) remains the gold standard for monitoring hepatotoxicity in psoriasis, as LFTs may be normal even with significant fibrosis. PIIINP is an alternative non-invasive marker used in some guidelines.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the buttocks and elbows, accompanied by intense pruritus. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal vesicles with neutrophils and eosinophils at the dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae. What is the underlying association?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease). Granular IgA deposits at dermal papillae tips on DIF is pathognomonic. Gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment; dapsone controls symptoms.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive symmetric proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over knuckles, and 'mechanic's hands'. Aldolase and CK are elevated. What is the most important investigation to exclude in this patient given the diagnosis?
opts: CT thorax for interstitial lung disease
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults has a significant association with underlying malignancy (ovarian, lung, colon, breast, nasopharyngeal cancers). A comprehensive malignancy workup (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET scan, tumour markers) is mandatory at diagnosis and annually for 3 years.

questions.q: A 50-year-old diabetic male presents with recurrent painful, erythematous swelling of the lower legs with fever, marking spreading despite oral antibiotics. On examination there is blistering and a clear demarcation line with proximal spread. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Add topical mupirocin and continue oral antibiotics
questions.exp: Spreading cellulitis with blistering and systemic signs in a diabetic patient not responding to oral antibiotics requires hospitalisation and IV antibiotics (penicillin/cefazolin for Group A Streptococcus or MSSA). Blood cultures should be taken before antibiotics.

questions.q: A newborn develops superficial blisters and crusting at the umbilical area within 3 days of birth. Gram stain of blister fluid shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Nikolsky's sign is positive. What is the underlying mechanism?
opts: Exfoliative toxins A and B produced by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) / Ritter's disease in neonates is caused by exfoliative toxins (ET-A, ET-B) produced by S. aureus phage group II. These toxins cleave desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, causing superficial blistering and positive Nikolsky's sign.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with multiple hyperpigmented macules on sun-exposed areas with irregular borders since childhood. She has a history of multiple basal cell carcinomas. Wood's lamp examination shows no enhancement. Which genodermatosis best explains this presentation?
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive disorder of nucleotide excision repair (NER), leading to sun sensitivity, multiple lentigines, and early-onset skin cancers (BCC, SCC, melanoma). Patients are unable to repair UV-induced DNA damage (pyrimidine dimers).

questions.q: A 27-year-old male presents with a 3 cm painless ulcer on the shaft of the penis with a shaggy, undermined edge and no induration. There is painful, matted inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Gram stain of bubo aspirate shows 'school of fish' pattern gram-negative bacilli. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: The presentation is chancroid caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. The 'school of fish' or 'railroad track' pattern on Gram stain is characteristic. Treatment options include ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 3 days, azithromycin 1 g single dose, ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose, or erythromycin 500 mg TDS for 7 days.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with a 20-year history of psoriasis involving >30% BSA and psoriatic arthritis fails methotrexate. He is started on adalimumab. Before initiation, which screening is MANDATORY?
opts: Tuberculin skin test (TST) or IGRA, hepatitis B and C serology, and chest X-ray
ECHO and baseline pulmonary function tests
questions.exp: Before initiating TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), screening for latent tuberculosis (TST or IGRA), active TB (CXR), hepatitis B and C is mandatory due to risk of reactivation and serious infections. LTBI must be treated before starting biologic therapy.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with an itchy, warty, brown-black plaque on the back with a 'stuck-on' appearance and visible pseudohorn cysts. Dermoscopy shows comedo-like openings and milium-like cysts. What is the histological hallmark?
opts: Acanthosis with horn cysts (pseudo-horn cysts) and papillomatosis
Nests of melanocytes at the DEJ
questions.exp: Seborrhoeic keratosis (seborrheic verruca) shows acanthosis, papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and characteristic horn cysts (true intraepidermal keratin-filled cysts) and pseudo-horn cysts (surface invaginations). These correlate dermoscopically with milium-like cysts and comedo-like openings.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with dusky-red, painful, tender nodules on the shins bilaterally. She also has fever, arthralgia, and hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. Serum ACE is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Erythema nodosum secondary to sarcoidosis (Löfgren syndrome)
questions.exp: Löfgren syndrome is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis characterised by erythema nodosum (bilateral, pretibial tender nodules), bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, fever, and arthralgia/arthritis — typically carries a good prognosis with spontaneous resolution.

questions.q: A 20-year-old medical student presents with scaly, pruritic patches in the scalp, eyebrows, and nasolabial folds. Yellowish, greasy scales are present. Wood's lamp shows no fluorescence. KOH is negative. What is the most likely pathogenesis?
opts: Cell-mediated immunity against house dust mite
Autoantibody production against cornified cell envelope
questions.exp: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is triggered by abnormal host immune response to Malassezia (Pityrosporum) species that colonise sebaceous gland-rich areas. Antifungals (ketoconazole, ciclopirox) and mild topical corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment.

questions.q: During patch testing, a patient shows a positive reaction (++) at 48 hours and 96 hours to nickel sulfate. Which cells primarily mediate this reaction?
opts: CD4+ Th1 lymphocytes and Langerhans cells
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (patch test reaction) is a Type IV (delayed-type, cell-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction. Langerhans cells (APCs) sensitise CD4+ Th1 T cells; on re-exposure, sensitised T cells release IFN-γ and TNF-α, causing the inflammatory response 48–96 hours later.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a firm, non-tender, flesh-coloured subcutaneous nodule on the forearm that appeared after trauma. Biopsy shows palisading histiocytes around a zone of degenerated collagen with mucin deposition. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Granuloma annulare shows palisading granulomas with central necrobiotic collagen and mucin on histology. Superficial GA presents as annular, skin-coloured to erythematous papules/plaques, often post-trauma. Deep (subcutaneous) GA can mimic a rheumatoid nodule but lacks rheumatoid factor and joint disease.

questions.q: A 40-year-old female presents with thickened, 'hide-bound' skin of the fingers (sclerodactyly), Raynaud's phenomenon, digital pitting scars, and telangiectasias. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. What complication should be monitored most closely?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) positivity strongly associates with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc / CREST syndrome). The most feared complication in ACA-positive lcSSc is pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), not renal crisis (which is more common in diffuse SSc with anti-Scl-70).

questions.q: A 29-year-old male presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery white scales on the scalp, elbows, and knees, with nail pitting and onycholysis. Auspitz sign is positive. Which cytokine is the primary driver of epidermal hyperproliferation in psoriasis?
questions.exp: IL-17A, produced predominantly by Th17 cells, is the central cytokine driving keratinocyte hyperproliferation, neutrophil recruitment, and the inflammatory cascade in psoriasis. This is the rationale for the efficacy of IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) in psoriasis.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman is being treated for onychomycosis with terbinafine 250 mg daily. At 6 weeks she reports loss of taste and smell. What is the recommended action?
opts: Reduce dose to 125 mg daily and continue
Discontinue terbinafine and switch to itraconazole pulse therapy
Add zinc supplementation and continue terbinafine
Continue terbinafine — taste disturbance is not a recognised side effect
questions.exp: Taste disturbance (dysgeusia/ageusia) and smell disturbance (anosmia) are recognised, albeit uncommon, adverse effects of terbinafine that may persist or be irreversible. The drug should be discontinued and an alternative antifungal (e.g., itraconazole pulse therapy 200 mg BD for 1 week per month) should be considered.

questions.q: A 17-year-old presents with recurring episodes of erythema, vesiculation, and crusting at the same site on the lips each time he takes ibuprofen. The lesion heals with slate-grey hyperpigmentation. What is the name for this reaction and its mechanism?
opts: Stevens-Johnson syndrome — IgE-mediated Type I hypersensitivity
Fixed drug eruption — CD8+ T cells retained in skin at the lesional site, reactivated by the drug
Toxic epidermal necrolysis — widespread keratinocyte apoptosis via FasL
Lichenoid drug eruption — Type IV delayed hypersensitivity to drug-modified keratinocytes
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption (FDE) recurs at the same site with each drug challenge. Intraepidermal CD8+ T cells (effector memory T cells) persist at the site and are reactivated by the offending drug (NSAIDs, tetracyclines, sulphonamides, paracetamol are common causes). The hallmark post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is due to melanin-laden macrophages.

questions.q: A 38-year-old HIV-positive female with CD4 count of 45 cells/µL presents with wart-like verrucous plaques over the perineum, buttocks, and trunk. Biopsy shows large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies and thickened epidermis without granulomas. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: In severe immunosuppression (CD4 <100), molluscum contagiosum may present as giant (>5 mm) or confluent verrucous plaques rather than discrete umbilicated papules. Histology shows Henderson-Paterson (molluscum) bodies — large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies in the spinous and granular layers — confirming MCV.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a painless, indurated, non-healing ulcer on the lower lip for 8 months, with surface covered by crusting. He is a chronic smoker and farmer. Biopsy shows dysplastic squamous cells invading the dermis with keratin pearl formation. What is the MOST important prognostic factor?
questions.exp: For cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), perineural invasion is one of the most important adverse prognostic factors associated with local recurrence, lymph node metastasis, and disease-specific mortality. It is a high-risk feature per AJCC staging.

questions.q: A dermatology resident performs a punch biopsy for suspected lichen planus. Which layer of the epidermis is characteristically damaged in lichen planus, and what is the histological hallmark?
opts: Stratum granulosum — loss of the granular layer
Stratum basale — vacuolar degeneration of basal cells with apoptotic keratinocytes (Civatte/colloid bodies) and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate
Stratum spinosum — acantholysis above the basal layer
Stratum corneum — parakeratosis with neutrophilic exudate
questions.exp: Lichen planus shows: (1) hyperkeratosis with wedge-shaped hypergranulosis, (2) band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ, (3) vacuolar degeneration of basal cells, (4) Civatte bodies (apoptotic keratinocytes), and (5) saw-tooth rete ridges. The basal layer is the primary target.

questions.q: A 24-year-old female presents with painful genital vesicles and ulcers, dysuria, fever, and inguinal lymphadenopathy. She is 30 weeks pregnant. PCR confirms HSV-2. What is the most appropriate management to prevent neonatal herpes?
opts: Oral acyclovir 400 mg TDS for 7–10 days; monitor clinically
Oral acyclovir 400 mg TDS for treatment, then acyclovir 400 mg BD from 36 weeks until delivery; offer elective caesarean if lesions at labour
Valacyclovir 1 g BD for 10 days; no further prophylaxis required
Topical acyclovir cream only; caesarean delivery is mandatory regardless
questions.exp: In primary genital herpes in pregnancy, the standard approach is: treat the acute episode with oral acyclovir (400 mg TDS for 10 days), then suppressive acyclovir 400 mg BD from 36 weeks gestation until delivery to reduce viral shedding and lesion recurrence at the time of labour. Caesarean section is recommended if active lesions are present at the onset of labour.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with recurrent crops of tense blisters on the oral mucosa, esophagus, and skin, with crusted erosions. DIF shows IgG and C3 deposits in an 'n-serration' pattern on the dermal side of salt-split skin (floor of split). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (EBA) targets Type VII collagen (anchoring fibrils beneath the lamina densa). On salt-split skin, IgG deposits on the dermal floor (n-serration pattern on electron microscopy). EBA presents with mechanobullous (non-inflammatory) or inflammatory variants with tense bullae, milia, and scarring.

questions.q: A 25-year-old female presents with a 2-year history of recurrent oral and genital ulcers, erythema nodosum, anterior uveitis, and pathergy test positivity. What is the recommended test to confirm pathergy, and which HLA antigen is associated?
opts: Patch test with nickel sulfate; HLA-DR4
Intradermal injection of 0.1 mL saline — pustule formation at 48 hours; HLA-B51
Prick test with Candida antigen; HLA-B27
Patch test with 1% potassium dichromate; HLA-B35
questions.exp: Behçet's disease is confirmed by the International Study Group criteria (recurrent oral ulcers + 2 of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions, positive pathergy test). Pathergy is tested by intradermal pricking/injection of saline — an erythematous papule or pustule at 48 hours is positive. HLA-B51 is strongly associated with Behçet's disease, especially in populations along the old 'Silk Road'.
